plan: Literary narrative of about 520 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000017) with a first-person narrator of unstated gender; two hard items (synthesizing two actions; composure versus indifference).

passages.title: Keep It Sharp
passages.text:
For my first three months at the Brass Lantern, Chef Albescu said exactly four words to me that were not instructions. They were "Your knives are dull," and she said them on my first morning, in front of the entire kitchen, after watching me struggle through a crate of onions.

I sharpened the knives that night and every night after. I learned to dice an onion in the time it took the dishwasher to fill a sink. I learned that a sauce should coat the back of a spoon and hold a clean line when you drew a finger through it, and that Albescu could tell from across the room whether it would. She never said whether mine did. She would taste, set the spoon down, and move on, and I would spend the rest of the shift trying to read her silence.

Some nights I resented her for it. I would walk home past the bakery on Ninth Street, already dark, and rehearse speeches I would never give: that I had been cooking since I was twelve, that my grandmother had taught me to braise, that no one could be expected to improve without being told what was wrong. By morning the speeches seemed foolish, and I would be back at my station before anyone else, sharpening.

The other cooks had a theory about her. Albescu, they said, had trained in a kitchen in Lyon where praise was considered a kind of laziness, a way of telling a cook to stop improving. Whether that was true, no one knew. She never talked about Lyon, or about anything else that had happened before she bought the restaurant.

In my fourth month, a critic from the city paper came in unannounced. We knew who he was only because the host recognized him and came back to the kitchen white-faced. Two of the line cooks stopped working altogether, and someone dropped a pan. Albescu didn't look up. She finished plating the dish in front of her and then, without a word, slid the critic's ticket down the line to my station. It was the braised lamb, my dish, the one I had made every night for six weeks.

I don't remember cooking it. I remember the plate leaving the kitchen and the hum of the dining room and Albescu's back, which did not move. The review ran on Sunday, and I read it standing up in the tiny kitchen of my apartment. It praised the lamb in a single sentence and spent three paragraphs on the dessert, which I had not made.

On Monday I came in early, as I always did, and found a new knife at my station, a heavy carbon-steel blade wrapped in a clean dish towel. There was no note. When Albescu came in an hour later, she glanced at the knife, then at me. "Keep it sharp," she said, and went to check the walk-in cooler. I used that knife for eleven years, and I have it still.

candidates.stem: Taken together, Albescu's decision about the critic's ticket (paragraph 5) and the knife left at the narrator's station (paragraph 7) most strongly suggest that she:

choices.A: wanted to see whether the narrator would fail when the pressure was greatest.
choices.B: showed confidence in the narrator through actions rather than words.
choices.C: regretted that the critic had praised the dessert more than the narrator's dish.
choices.D: planned to make the narrator the head cook of the restaurant in the near future.

candidates.evidence: slid the critic's ticket down the line to my station
candidates.explanation: She trusts the narrator with the critic's order and later gives a fine knife, both without praise: actions that express confidence.

A.rationale: The knife afterward suggests approval, not a test the narrator was expected to fail.

C.rationale: Nothing shows Albescu reacting to the review's emphasis.

D.rationale: No promotion is mentioned or implied.

hints: What do the two actions have in common?
Does Albescu ever say anything approving?
candidates.remember: Characters who rarely speak reveal judgments through actions.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires combining two widely separated actions; considering paragraph 5 alone makes the "test" reading (A) tempting.

candidates.stem: The fourth paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: offer a possible explanation for Albescu's silence that cannot be confirmed.
choices.B: reveal the real reason Albescu never praised the cooks who worked for her.
choices.C: describe in detail the training Albescu received in a kitchen in Lyon.
choices.D: show that the other cooks disliked Albescu and resented her strict methods.

candidates.evidence: Whether that was true, no one knew
candidates.explanation: The cooks' theory explains her silence, but the paragraph stresses that no one could confirm it.

B.rationale: "Whether that was true, no one knew"; the explanation is unconfirmed.

C.rationale: The paragraph reports a rumor, not details of her training.

D.rationale: The cooks have a theory about her; no dislike is described.

hints: Does the paragraph present a fact or a theory?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that treat the rumor as fact.

candidates.remember: Function questions: notice how certain the passage is about what it reports.

candidates.stem: The narrator's statement about spending "the rest of the shift trying to read her silence" (paragraph 2) suggests that the narrator:

choices.A: had trouble hearing Albescu's instructions over the kitchen noise.
choices.B: was relieved that Albescu offered no comments on the sauces.
choices.C: had stopped caring what Albescu thought of the cooking.
choices.D: cared about Albescu's judgment and looked for any sign of it.

candidates.evidence: She never said whether mine did
candidates.explanation: Spending a shift interpreting her silence shows how much the narrator wanted her approval.

A.rationale: "Read her silence" is figurative; it is not about hearing.

B.rationale: Trying to read her silence suggests anxiety, not relief.

C.rationale: Spending a whole shift interpreting her shows the opposite.

hints: Why would someone spend hours interpreting silence?
candidates.remember: Figurative phrases often reveal a character's preoccupations.

candidates.subskill: Inferring the purpose of a detail
candidates.stem: The narrator mentions that the review spent three paragraphs on the dessert, "which I had not made" (paragraph 6), most likely to suggest that:

choices.A: the lamb the narrator cooked that night had been poorly made.
choices.B: the dessert had always been the narrator's favorite part of the menu.
choices.C: the narrator's dish received little public recognition.
choices.D: Albescu had made the dessert herself to impress the critic.

candidates.evidence: praised the lamb in a single sentence
candidates.explanation: One sentence for the lamb against three paragraphs for someone else's dessert: the narrator's work got little public credit, which sets up Albescu's private gesture.

A.rationale: The review "praised the lamb"; it was not criticized.

B.rationale: Nothing indicates the narrator's preferences about the menu.

D.rationale: The passage never says who made the dessert.

hints: How much of the review was about the narrator's dish?

strategy.explanation: Compare the space given to each dish.

candidates.remember: Details placed side by side often imply a contrast.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the cooks knew that the critic was in the restaurant because:

choices.A: Albescu had been warned that he would come.
choices.B: the host recognized him and told the kitchen.
choices.C: his name was printed on the order ticket.
choices.D: the narrator had seen his photograph in the paper.

candidates.explanation: Paragraph 5: "the host recognized him and came back to the kitchen white-faced."

C.rationale: Nothing says his name was on the ticket.

D.rationale: Only the host is said to have recognized him.

hints: Reread the second sentence of paragraph 5.
candidates.remember: Detail questions: the answer is stated in the passage.

candidates.stem: Albescu's behavior when the critic arrives (paragraph 5) most strongly suggests that she is:

choices.A: indifferent to whether the restaurant receives a good review.
choices.B: nervous and too distracted to cook the critic's dish herself.
choices.C: eager to impress the critic by greeting him personally.
choices.D: calm and focused even under pressure.

candidates.explanation: While the host panics, Albescu keeps working and makes a deliberate choice about the ticket: composure under pressure.

A.rationale: She hands the order to a trusted cook; staying calm is not the same as not caring.

B.rationale: She "didn't look up" and finished her plate; nothing suggests nerves.

C.rationale: She stays in the kitchen and does not greet him.

hints: How does her reaction contrast with the host's?

author_checklist.hardness: Choice A (indifference) fits her outward behavior; ruling it out requires weighing the deliberate handoff of the critic's order.

candidates.stem: The narrator's statement "I don't remember cooking it" (paragraph 6) most likely conveys:

choices.A: that someone else secretly cooked the dish while the narrator watched.
choices.B: that the narrator had cooked the lamb so often that it no longer mattered.
choices.C: how intense and absorbing the moment of cooking for the critic was.
choices.D: that the narrator was later ashamed of how the dish had turned out.

candidates.evidence: I remember the plate leaving the kitchen
candidates.explanation: The narrator remembers only the plate leaving and Albescu's still back: the pressure blotted out the cooking itself.

A.rationale: The dish was the narrator's, sent to the narrator's station.

B.rationale: The surrounding details show the moment mattered greatly.

D.rationale: The review praised the lamb; no shame is suggested.

hints: What does the narrator remember instead?
candidates.remember: Memory gaps in a narrative often signal intensity.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, how long had the narrator been making the braised lamb when the critic came?
candidates.evidence: the one I had made every night for six weeks
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 5 says the narrator had made the lamb "every night for six weeks."

B.rationale: The critic came in the narrator's fourth month at the restaurant, not after four months of the lamb.

C.rationale: Three months is how long Albescu said nothing but instructions.

hints: Reread the last sentence of paragraph 5.

strategy.explanation: Scan for a length of time.

candidates.remember: Watch for nearby numbers that answer a different question.

withdrawn.reason: Both blind solvers flagged that it tests the same phrase ("read her silence") as R017-03, so each cues the other. Withdrawn after the blind solve and before review.

item.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
item.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "read" most nearly means:
item.explanation: To "read" a silence is to interpret what it means.

B.rationale: Reciting means saying aloud, which does not fit silence.

C.rationale: Studying suggests reviewing material, not interpreting a reaction.

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the phrase.

item.remember: Context fixes which meaning of a common word is used.
